stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene before cannulating a client's arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis. Which additional infection-prevention principle is essential?

options.A: Use clean technique for fistula cannulation because bloodstream-infection prevention measures are needed only when a dialysis catheter is accessed.
options.B: Skip access-site preparation when the fistula skin appears intact because visible cleanliness is sufficient after hand hygiene.
options.C: Reuse a vascular-access needle for the same client if it remains visibly clean because repeated cannulation does not require a new sterile device each time.
options.D: Use aseptic technique for vascular-access cannulation and follow standardized access-care practices each time the fistula is used.

rationale: CDC dialysis-safety resources emphasize staff education and competency in vascular-access care and aseptic technique, and CDC provides specific AV fistula/graft cannulation checklists. More broadly, CDC intravascular-access guidance requires aseptic technique for insertion and care. D correctly adds aseptic access care to hand hygiene. A incorrectly limits infection-prevention measures to catheters, B omits access-site preparation based on appearance alone, and C proposes unsafe reuse of an access needle.
educational_objective: Use aseptic technique and standardized vascular-access practices whenever an AV fistula is cannulated for hemodialysis.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention in Dialysis Setting; Dialysis Safety Resources & Tools
source_locator: Core Interventions — Catheter/vascular access care observations and Staff education and competency; Resources & Tools — AV Fistula & Graft Cannulation and Decannulation Audit Tool/Checklist; CDC intravascular catheter guidance — Hand Hygiene and Aseptic Technique.
source_claim_supported: Dialysis infection prevention requires trained, competent vascular-access care using aseptic technique; CDC maintains standardized AV fistula/graft cannulation tools and requires aseptic technique for vascular-access care.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

source_original.stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene before cannulating a client's arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis. Which additional infection-prevention principle is essential?

options.A: Use clean technique for fistula cannulation because bloodstream-infection prevention measures are needed only when a dialysis catheter is being accessed.
options.B: Skip access-site preparation when the fistula skin appears intact, because visible cleanliness is sufficient after the nurse has completed hand hygiene.
options.C: Reuse a vascular-access needle for the same client if it remains visibly clean, because repeated cannulation does not require a new sterile device each time.
options.D: Use aseptic technique whenever the vascular access is cannulated and follow the facility's standardized access-care practices each time the fistula is used.

source_original.rationale: Hand hygiene is necessary, but CDC dialysis-safety guidance also emphasizes aseptic vascular-access care and staff competency. Option D correctly adds aseptic technique and standardized access practices to hand hygiene. Option A incorrectly limits aseptic precautions to dialysis catheters. Option B skips access-site preparation based on appearance alone. Option C proposes reuse of a vascular-access needle, which is inconsistent with sterile single-use access practice.
source_original.source_detail: CDC Dialysis Safety — Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention: staff training and competency in vascular-access care and aseptic technique; observe adherence to aseptic technique during vascular-access care/cannulation. Current CDC dialysis-safety clinical guidance at cited URL; rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: asepsis, equipment/environmental safety, incident/event prevention and infection-control activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained key and construct. Removed the unnecessary phrase tying the correct answer to a facility-specific standard alone and anchored it to CDC aseptic vascular-access care plus CDC's standardized AV fistula/graft cannulation tools.

audit_findings.currentness: CDC dialysis resources updated March 2024 and current in 2026.
audit_findings.exact_locator: Core Interventions vascular-access care/staff competency; AV fistula/graft cannulation tools; aseptic-technique recommendation.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final key uses only aseptic vascular-access and standardized-care principles; no antiseptic agent, dwell time or glove type is invented.

distractor_audit.B: Visible cleanliness does not replace access-site preparation/aseptic care.

audit_findings.cueing: All options concern infection prevention at cannulation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Confirmed no unsupported skin-antisepsis specifics were added and no second answer remains.
